claims.claim: pd.merge_asof defaults to direction="backward" and allow_exact_matches=True.
claims.source: pandas API reference; run on pandas 3.0.6 in this repository.

concept_html:
When rows have dates, every feature must be computed as of the row's own date, using only earlier data. Three tools in pandas 3.0 cover most cases.

Prior-only aggregates. "Total spend before this order" must exclude the current order. Take the running total and subtract the current value, or shift first:

orders = orders.sort_values(["customer", "ordered_at"])
prior = orders.groupby("customer")["spend"].cumsum() - orders["spend"]

Point-in-time joins. To attach the latest satisfaction score before each prediction date, use pd.merge_asof. It matches each left row with the last right row whose key is at or before it, within the same by group. Both frames must be sorted on the key.

pd.merge_asof(preds.sort_values("as_of"), scores.sort_values("scored_at"),
              left_on="as_of", right_on="scored_at", by="customer",
              allow_exact_matches=False)

The default allow_exact_matches=True also matches a score recorded at the same timestamp as the prediction. If that score could only be known after the prediction was made, set it to False. A plain merge on customer followed by "take the latest" silently uses scores from the future.

Time-based splits. Random splits put next month's rows in training and last month's in test. For anything you will use forward in time, split by date: train on data up to a cut-off, test on data after it. scikit-learn's TimeSeriesSplit gives expanding windows for cross-validation.

Build a small as-of test for every time feature: a customer with events before and after the prediction date, and an assertion that only the earlier events count. It catches most mistakes in a few lines.

lines: import pandas as pd
def add_prior_spend(orders: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
"""Spend and order count before each order, per customer. Grain: one row per order."""
o = orders.sort_values(["customer", "ordered_at"])
grp = o.groupby("customer")["spend"]
prior_spend=grp.cumsum() - o["spend"],
prior_orders=o.groupby("customer").cumcount(),
def time_split(df: pd.DataFrame, date_col: str, cutoff: pd.Timestamp) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.DataFrame]:
"""Train on rows before cutoff, test on rows at or after it."""
before = df[date_col] < cutoff
return df[before], df[~before]

exercises.solution:
import pandas as pd


def add_prior_spend(orders: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Spend and order count before each order, per customer.

    Args:
        orders: Columns customer, ordered_at, spend.

    Returns:
        Orders sorted by customer and date, with prior_spend and prior_orders.
    """
    o = orders.sort_values(["customer", "ordered_at"])
    return o.assign(
        prior_spend=o.groupby("customer")["spend"].cumsum() - o["spend"],
        prior_orders=o.groupby("customer").cumcount(),
    )

def latest_nps(preds: pd.DataFrame, scores: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
"""Most recent NPS strictly before each prediction date."""
joined = preds.merge(scores, on="customer")

title: Time-safe features and point-in-time joins
why_html:
A next-purchase model used "customer's total orders" as a feature, computed once over the full order table. For each training row, the count included orders placed after the row's date, including the very purchase the model was trying to predict. Validation AUC was 0.91. In production, where the future does not exist yet, it was 0.68.

Recomputing the count as prior orders only brought validation down to 0.70. That was the model's true performance, and the team finally had an honest number to improve.
